newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU fails to agree on postal liberalisation.
newsitem.headline: EU fails to agree on postal liberalisation.

text.p: European Union ministers failed to reach a deal on Thursday on when and how to open EU postal services to competition, EU officials said.
The deadlock prompted the European Commission to warn that it might be forced to act on its own to apply EU fair-competition rules to the postal sector.
The post and telecommunications ministers were mainly divided over the question of when to end the monopolies of state post offices over direct or "junk" mail and cross-border mail.
They were unable to bridge the gap between a Franco-German camp that did not want to set a firm date for opening those sectors and others who favoured setting a timetable.

"A complex combination of national concerns and domestic politics in certain member states made agreement impossible," Irish Telecommunications Minister Michael Lowry, who chaired the meeting, told a news conference.
France, mindful of strikes that paralysed the country a year ago and wary of inciting new public unrest, has led an effort to delay significant postal liberalisation in the immediate future.
It argues that too many jobs are at stake and that brutal liberalisation could lead to a deterioration of "universal service", or basic postal service to all residents.

But the Commission is under pressure from the direct mail industry, express operators and others to chip away at state postal monopolies. Industry Commissioner Martin Bangemann told a news conference that it was obliged under the EU treaty to respond to their concerns.

"We already have complaints," he told the news conference. "And you can easily foresee that with the non-decision of today, more parties that may have been hoping for a clarification of their legal system will apply and complain to the Commission."

But French Telecommunications Minister Francois Fillon warned that the Franco-German initiative, which would freeze liberalisation of direct and cross-border mail until at least 2003, had won the support of nine countries.
He told reporters the Commission could not ignore that "balance of power".
Austria, Britain, Denmark, Finland, the Netherlands and Sweden opposed the final Franco-German text that was put on the table -- representing enough votes to block it.
The European Commission, which argues that state post offices must become more competitive in an era of electronic mail and faxes, had originally proposed a two-step liberalisation process.
Countries would first allow competition to deliver mail weighing more than 350 grams and costing more than five times the tariff for a standard letter -- an uncontroversial step.
They would liberalise direct mail and incoming cross-border by 2001. The plan would have liberalised just under 25 percent of EU mail by volume.
France and Germany argued against any automatic liberalisation and wanted to ensure that no action would be taken before 2003.

Germany surprised its EU partners by agreeing to support France, despite plans to liberalise its own postal sector. Post Minister Wolfgang Boetsch told reporters on Thursday that he was supporting France out of a sense of solidarity, saying "it's a piece in the mosaic of the Franco-German relationship."

The European Express Organisation issued a statement after the meeting calling on the Commission to publish a notice that it has been drafting on how it will apply competition rules to the postal sector.
The Commission has said that it would publish the notice by the end of 1996, with or without an accord by ministers.
